item: 1. DDIM (Song, Meng, Ermon)
quote: "We empirically demonstrate that DDIMs can produce high quality samples 10x to 50x faster in terms of wall-clock time compared to DDPMs" (abstract). Sec 5.1: "DDIM is able to produce samples with quality comparable to 1000 step models within 20 to 100 steps, which is a 10x to 50x speed up compared to the original DDPM."

quote: Abstract: "new state-of-the-art FID of 1.79 for CIFAR-10 in a class-conditional setting and 1.97 in an unconditional setting, with much faster sampling (35 network evaluations per image) ... improving the FID of a previously trained ImageNet-64 model from 2.07 to near-SOTA 1.55, and after re-training with our proposed improvements to a new SOTA of 1.36." Why stochasticity helps (Sec 4): "The implicit Langevin diffusion drives the sample towards the desired marginal distribution at a given time, actively correcting for any errors made in earlier sampling steps. On the other hand, approximating the Langevin term with discrete SDE solver steps introduces error in itself." Also: "Increasing the amount of stochasticity is effective in correcting errors made by earlier sampling steps, but it has its own drawbacks" (loss of detail, drift to oversaturated colours).
location: Abstract; Table 1 'Ours (EDM)' column (Sampling, Network and preconditioning, Training, Parameters rows); Table 2 config F; Table 3; Table 4 'Alg. 2, Optimal settings'; Table 5 (stochastic sampling parameters); Figures 5c, 6, 7; Section 4 'Practical considerations'.

Safe statement: on ImageNet-64 their retrained model goes from 2.23 (deterministic, 79 NFE) to 1.36 (stochastic, 511 NFE); the pretrained ADM goes from 2.64 (deterministic) to 1.55 (stochastic). Also on CIFAR-10 with their own training stochasticity is 'not only unnecessary but harmful' (Fig 5b caption).

CFG: "We empirically find w=7.5, phi=0.7 works great." Offset noise: "Offset noise does enable Stable Diffusion model to generate very bright and dark samples but it is incongruent with the theory of the diffusion process and may generate samples with brightness that does not fit the true data distribution, i.e. too bright or too dark. item: 13. Offset noise (Nicholas Guttenberg, Cross Labs blog)
version_read: web page fetched 2026-10-17 (page now titled 'Cross Labs Historical Research Archive')

numbers.base: fine-tuned SD 1.5; fine-tuning on a single black image for 3000 steps failed to produce black images without the trick

quote: "The issue turns out to be that you don't ever completely erase the original image during the forward process, so in turn the reverse model starting from pure noise doesn't exactly get back to the complete true distribution of images." On 0.1: "the choice of 0.1 there worked well for me given my limited data and training time - if I made it too large it'd tend to dominate too much of the model's existing behavior, but much smaller and I wouldn't see an improvement". Request: "please incorporate a little bit of offset noise like this into the training process the next time you do a big run."
location: Blog post body; code snippet; concluding paragraph.
notes: The post says SD outputs average 'relatively close to 0.5' brightness. Two loose statements in the post: it says the std of independent noise samples 'scales like 1/N' (it is 1/sqrt(N)) and counts SD latents as '3 x 64^2 = 12288' dimensions (SD latents have 4 channels). Lin et al. 2023 later argue offset noise is a trick that does not fix the root cause (non-zero terminal SNR).

item: 14. Meng et al. 'On Distillation of Guided Diffusion Models'
version_read: v3 PDF (12 Apr 2023; CVPR 2023) plus ar5iv

numbers.method: stage 1: a single w-conditioned student matches the combined conditional + unconditional (CFG) output, so one forward pass replaces two; stage 2: progressive distillation to fewer steps

"... while being up to 256 times faster to sample from."

notes: Internal inconsistency in speedup wording for latent models: abstract 'accelerating inference by at least 10-fold', Figure 1 'reduce the total number of sampling steps by at least 20x'.

item: 18. Imagen (Saharia et al. 2022) dynamic thresholding

numbers.definition: at each step set s to a percentile of |x0_hat| (per sample); if s > 1, clip x0_hat to [-s, s] and divide by s

quote: "increasing the classifier-free guidance weight improves image-text alignment, but damages image fidelity producing highly saturated and unnatural images ... high guidance weights cause x-predictions to exceed these bounds. This is a train-test mismatch". "Dynamic thresholding: ... at each sampling step we set s to a certain percentile absolute pixel value in x0_hat, and if s>1, then we threshold x0_hat to the range [-s,s] and then divide by s. Dynamic thresholding pushes saturated pixels (those near -1 and 1) inwards, thereby actively preventing pixels from saturation at each step."

notes: The main text does not state the percentile; 99.5 appears only in the appendix figure caption. Static thresholding = clip to [-1, 1]. Pseudo-code writes jnp.max(s, 1.0) where jnp.maximum is meant (cosmetic).
